to hear the Secretary in that Department in the matter. 
At its next meeting held on 2nd June, 1979 the Commillce heard

tives informed the Committee the circumstances under which ad­
hoc arrangements were made. They said that the incumbent hold 
ing the post got a job in some other department in a highc1· grade

tised for regular recruitment Thus, departmental candidates wer" 
considered by the Departmental Promotion Committee which select­
ed the next senior most person though he was not a graduate but 
had 9 years' technical experience. The incumbent who went to an 
outside office resigned in December, 1978 and the post was advertis­
ed for making regular appointment. As there was no graduate in 
the 'Library ad-hoc arrangements were made

jection taken by the Committee, gave an assurance to fulfil the 
following stlggcstions vi~.-
" (l) To plnce the mo.tter before the Governing Body to regu­
larise the appointment held by the incumbent on ad hoc 
basis and to regularise it in a manner lhat lhe fellow may 
not have to return the money for the period for which he 
held the post on ad hoc basis. 
(2) To fUl up the post on regular basis in accordance with 
the provisions of the recruitment rules.

(3) To issue instructions to the autonomous organisations not 
to repeat such cases.

MEMORANDUM 
SuBJECT: Sixty-Fourth Raport of the Public Accounts Committee 
(Fourth Lok Sabha)~Statutory Control over Govern­
ment's borrowing 
The Public Accounts Committee in para 1.11 of their Sixty­
Fourth Report have made the following recommendation:-
"The Committee have carefully 1considered the arguments put 
forward by Government for not accepting their repeated 
suggestion that a practical trial should be given to the 
healthy principle enunciated in Article 292 of the Cons­
titution for fixing a Limit by Parliament on Public 
borrowings. ·The country is now committed to planning 
on a five-years basis. This necessary presupposes a 
long-term assessment of resources needed for develop­
mental effort and the extent to whkh such resources 
should be raised through additional taxation 
borrowing and deficit financing. It should, there­
fore, be possible to vvork out with a reasonable degree of 
approximation a workable limit on borrowings for pur­
pose of incorporation in a statute as contemplated in 
Article 292 of the Constitution. The Committee would 
like Government to reconsider their position in the light 
of the foregoing considerations. 
2. The reasons for which the Government found it difficult tc. 
accept the earlier recommendations of the Public Accounts Commit­
tee had been explained in the Memorandum dated 29th January, 
27 

1967 submitted to the 
below:~ 
28 
Committee. These are briefly recounted 
"(i) The constitutional provision regarding Government's 
borrowings is permissive and not mandatory (Article 
292). 
(ii) Broad limits of the net borrowing proposed over a Plan 
periorl through domestic market loans from Reserve 
Bank, and through Budgetary receipts corresponding to 
external assistance . are generally indicated in the Plan 
documents. 
(iii) The borrowings proposed during the ensuing financial 
year by various categori>es are shown distinctly in the 
Budget presented to Parliament. 
The budget documents, of course, do not indicate the timing a;; 
well as the terms and conditions of the proposed borrow­
ings nor would it be possible to do so even if there is to 
be any statutory provision in regard to limits, etc. 
(iv) :Parliament has ample opportunity to discuss the pro­
posed borrowings by Government (a) over a plan period 
and (b) also during this ensuing financial year when it 
discusses the plan and the annual Budget. Moreover, in 
the ultimate analysis Government's borrowings from all 
sources are limited by the supply gr~nted by Parliament, 
the re~uirements for which cannot be raised through 
sources like Revenue etc. 
(v) Limits on borrowings from Reserve Bank present. special 
problem. These vary not only from year to year but even 
from time to time during· a year itself, 8Jccording to cir­
cumstances, needs and other considerations. It is only 
the net borrowing over a year which is of significance 
but any enactment in regard to limits would have to be 
with reference to the maximum amount of borrowing at 
any time and not the net over the year and this would be 
misleading. 
(vi) Limits on external borrowings would be even more 
difficult. The extent of such borrowings depends on the 
prevailing circumstances and involve p~tient negotiat:io~s. 
It would not be desirable or even practicable to put hm1tls 
on such borrowings halving regard to the factors which 
affect external assistance. 

, .. 
• 29 
(vii) If borrowirigs from. Reserve Bank and foreign loans are 
left out, any legislative approval for the residuary borrow~ 
ings will have little significance. 
(viii) If notwithstanding the foregoing consideration sta­
tutory limits. are though necessary, these would have to 
be sufficiently wide so that the need for frequent amend·· 
~·· ments to the statute does not arise. On the other hand, 
such wide limits:-which are by and large already set by 
the Plan documents and the annual Budgets-will serve 
no practical purpose. Statutory limits would, therefore, 
confer no advantage but on the other hand hamper the 
flexibility which is now available: 
3. In their latest recommendation contained in para 1.11 of the 
Sixty-Fourth Report (Fourth Lok Sabha), the Public Accounts 
Committee have suggested that a workable limit on borrowings can 
be incorporated in a st~atute in the light of the assessment of re­
sources made for the purpose of Five Year Plan. The assessment of 
resources made in the Five Year Plan is based on certain assump­
tions and is apt to be affected by development not foreseeable at the 
time of formulation of the Plan. For example, there ' were wide 
Yvariations between the scheme of financJng contemplated in the 
Third Plan and the actuals. The assumptions made in the Five 
Year Plans cannot, therefore, be taken as firm basis for fixing sta~ 
tutory limits on borrowings. The Five Year Plan is reviewed 
annually and the annual Plan and the annual Budget reflect the 
latest estimates for the year in regard to the debt to be incurred 
under various heads. But these too are subject to fluctuations. 
4. Parliament is Kept fully apprised of tihe borrowing of the 
Government. In fact, the Budget documents show not only the 
details of the borrowing programme for the Budget Year by cate­
gories, but also of the growth of Public Debt ever since 1950-51 vide 
Statement VI in Section II of Part II of tihe Explanatory Memo­
randum on the Budget. Moreover, in the ultimate analysis, Govern­
ment's borrowings are even now limited indirectly by the Parlia­
ment, year to year, by setting limits to the total expenditure to be 
incurred by the Government. 
/ 5. In view of the reasons stated above 9overnment even after 
~~reconsidering the matter .are of the view that no real advan.tage 
will ,be served by. prescribing statutory limits on Government 
borrowings,

41The Committee, at its meeting held on the 21st October, 1980,

that the special procedure of examining defective currency notes

forwarded the comments received by them from the Reserve Bank 
of India, which ate reproduced below:~ 
"The tlajya Sabha Committee on Subordinate Legislation has, in 
its 43rd repOII't vide paragraph 39, raised the following. points, viz.-
(A) That the Special Procedure followed by the Bank in 
dealing with the claims in respect of charred, dilapidated or 
excessively soiled and brittle notes should form a part of the 
Reserve Bank of India (Note Refund) Rules, 1975; and 
(B) That the provision of appeal against the decision of the 
Prescribed Officer fBank may be introduced in the Reserve Bank 
of India (Note Refund) Rules, 1975. 
We set out below the Bank's comments on the aforementioned 
points. 
Regarding (A) 
Defective notes are disposed of in the following manner:-
(i) Those with slight mutilations· which are presented at tht' 
counters of the Bank are exchanged readily for good notes~ 
(ii) Those with mutilations which require closer scrutiny are 
. accepted by the Bank and the exchange value thereof paid if they 
are payable under the· Note Refund Rules. 
(iii) Notes which are charred, brittle or dilapidated are. sub. 
jected to scrutiny by several officials of the Reserve Bank . viz. 
first by those at the c<mnter, later at the junior level according to 
. the -powers delegated to them and subsequently, if necessary at 
the senior level viz. the Currency Officer who is t~e Prescribed 
Officer under the Bank's Note Refund Rules. These notes are, 

· therefGQ.'e, kept in the Sa.tne condition in wb,ich they are received 
an.d. . t4e tenderer is. advised to call at our office and witness the 
aqjudiaation of his/her notes if hejshe so desires and, if hejshe 
'does.not desire to be present the notes are adjudicated in hisfher 
absenae. In any case, the notes falling under this category are 
-also dealt with in the same m~nner in which the other notes are 
dealt with inasmuch as no special consideration is given and they 
are exchanged only if they are found payable under the Note 
Refund Rules. Therefore, no special treatment is given to the 
notes which are dealt with under Special Procedure but, in order 
to avoid . their .further dilapidation, they are dealt wi~ st,raight­
away by the Prescribed Officials in the presence of \1te other 
authorised officials of the Bank. 
Mutilated etc. notes for which value has been paid are subjected 
to a verification in the Bank's Verification Secti~n in view of what 
has been stated above, in re$pect of special procedure cases, those 
notes are not subjected to verification as the official concerned 
with the verification himself is present at the time of adjudication 
by the Currency Officer. 
Regarding (B) 
The other point raised by the Committee relates to the pro­
vision of appeal in the 1975 Rules against the decision of the 
Prescribed Officer/Bank. We presume the reference has been made 
to the provisions of rule 21 (2) of .the 1975 Rules. It may be point­
ed out in this connection that this rule is merely in the nature of a 
clarificatory provision and has been included to make It abundantly 
clear that the Prescribed Officer's or the Bank's decision in respect 
of a claim made under the 1975 Rules shall be final. It is necessary 
to retain this rule specially in the light of subsequent delegation, to· 
the public sector banks. It may be stated . that in terms of sub­
rule (2) of this Rule even though no appeal against the decision 
of the Prescribed Officer /Bank in regard to any claim therein shall 
lie the Prescribed Officer himself or the Bank itself is not precluded , . 
from reviewing its decision. The Bank has in this connection 
iSsued administrative instructions that if the Prescribed Officer (or 
the Central Office . of the Bank) is satisfied that a bonafide mistake 
has beeri made, it is open to him to correct the mistake either on 
his ·initiative or on his attention being drawn to the mistake by the 
claimant or any other person. 

23 
It may also be stated here that <.\ provision ol appttal cannot be 
sine qua-non of a good legislati-Qn, especially when by reason of 
section 28 of the Reserve Bank of India Act a claimant with a 
claim in respect of a mutilated or imperfect no~ has no right to­
recover the value of the note. It is :respectfully pointed out that 
the question whether the decision of ihe Prescribed Officer is objec­
tive or not, does not ¢1epend on a p·rovision for appeal against 
his decision. The Bank exercises sufficient · administrative control 
and supervision whenever requir~d. 
In this connection, we invite the attention of the. Committee to 
t~ followi~ passage in Helsbuty•s Laws of ltngland. 4th Edition. 
Vglum~ I paragraph 50 at page 54t ....... 
"50. Appe4Z l.f1'!1d review 
A right of appeal to a court or statutory tribunal is a cretiture 
of statute; there is no inherent right of appeal''. 
It will, therefore, be seen from the above that a right of appeai 
is not a natural right or an inherent right but is a creature of the 
rules. Therefore, the mere fact that rule 21 (2) provides that the 
claimant shall not have a right of tippeal against the decision of 
the Prescribed Officer or the Bank would not mean that ·there is 
any infringement of the. principles of natural justice. 
Attention is also invited to H.W.R. Wade's Administrative La~, 
4th Edition. page 566. The following pa~age is relevant:-
((Finality Claus.es: Many statutes provide that some decision 
,shall be ftnal. The courts have made it a rule that such provisions 
cannot hamper the operation of judicial control/' 
Therefore, the mere fact that rule 2·1 (2) provides that the 
decision of the Prescribed Officer /Bank shall be final . would not: 
mean that such decision will not be subject to judicial review. In 
fact, there have been several cases of parties going to Court and 
the Com:ts deciding the matter. 
Having regard to the facts that· there is no infringement of. the 
principles of natural justice and that the provision of rule 21 (2) 
cannot hamJ?.er the operation of judicial control, it is conside;red 
that provision of a right of appeal may not be quite nec~ssary."

visions contained in the R.B.I .. (Note Refund) Rules, 1975, flow

( 4) Unscientific nature of the amendment 
,, The amendment is totally unscientific in its approach. It assumes that 
the earlier limited disqualification had failed, and created a situation not 
conducive to the growth of co-operative movement. While changing a rule 
of law, there should be some basic and valid premise on which it is based. 
A rule of Jaw may not be changed simply because the executive so feels it 
without some valid policy reasons and without some materials in its posses­
sion warranting a change in the law. No such thing appears to be here. 
The amended rules were promulgated on 24th May, 1982, under 
Section 97(3) of the .Act. The rules are to be ~aid, as soon as may be 
after they are made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session, 
for a total period of 30 days, etc., and both Houses may agree to annul 
the rules. Accordingly, the amended rules were presumably laid before 
Parliament on 8th July, 1982 when the present Session began. In view 
of the unreasonableness of the amendment analysed above [Rule 59 (d)] 
it is requested that the amendment to the rule may be annulled.
